title: 第二十七章 地头蛇
content_zh:
身子彻底将养利索，已是半个月后。

    江砚重新支起了他那点小生计。城西坊市靠墙根的位置，秦伯替他讨了块巴掌大的地方，一张缺角的旧木桌，一只磨秃了的砚台，几张糙纸，就是他的全部家当。来往的贩夫走卒，有要给远方家里捎信的，有买卖记账算不清的，有官府贴了告示看不懂来问的，都能找他。一封信两文钱，记一笔账一文，遇上手头紧的，一碗热汤、半块饼也使得。

    日子紧巴，可总算是自己挣的。

    这天晌午，江砚正替一个贩盐的老汉写家书。老汉不识字，絮絮叨叨说着要给乡下婆娘捎的话，无非是“今年生意尚可”“勿念”“天冷添衣”，江砚一面听，一面拣要紧的落笔，把那些颠三倒四的家常话，理成几行通顺的字。

    笔走得稳。半个月没动那金手指，这阵子他天天就这么老老实实地写字、描帖，反倒觉出一种从前没有的安稳来。秦伯那番话像根刺，扎在心里，可扎得他踏实。

    坊市西头，忽然一阵骚动。

    先是有人压着嗓子喊了句什么，接着是摊子翻倒的哗啦声、铜钱滚落地的叮当声，再接着，是一个妇人带着哭腔的求告。

    江砚写字的手停了。

    写信的盐贩老汉脸色一变，慌忙缩了缩脖子，往江砚这边凑了凑，压低声音：“金牙的人……又来收钱了。先生你别看，低头写你的。”

    “金牙？”

    “坊市里的地头蛇。”老汉的声音抖着，眼睛却忍不住往那头瞟，“嘴里镶了颗金牙，谁见了都得喊一声‘金牙爷’。这西市口，明里是官府的市，暗里——是他的。摆摊的，进货的，连讨饭的，都得给他‘孝敬’。给晚了、给少了，轻则砸摊子，重则打断腿。”

    江砚顺着声音望过去。

    二十来步外，三四个膀大腰圆的汉子，正围着一个卖针头线脑的中年妇人。当中一个，矮胖，敞着怀，露出一身横肉，张口说话，嘴里那颗金牙在日头下晃得人眼晕。他脚下踩着翻倒的货摊，针线、纽扣、零碎的布头撒了一地，那妇人跪在地上，一边手忙脚乱地往回拢，一边哭着求。

    “金牙爷，这月……这月实在凑不齐啊。我家那口子病着，孩子还小……”

    “病着？”金牙啐了一口，“病着你还出来摆摊？摆摊就是有进项。有进项凭啥不孝敬爷？”他一脚把刚拢起的一小堆货又踢散，“规矩就是规矩。今儿三十文，一文不能少。凑不齐？凑不齐爷帮你凑——”

    他一挥手，旁边的汉子上去就要掀那妇人最后护着的一个小布包。

    “别动!别动那个!那是给我家娃抓药的钱啊——”

    妇人扑上去护，被一把推开，跌坐在地。

    满坊市的人,没一个敢上前。摆摊的低着头收拾自己的货，过路的脚步加快了往别处绕，连方才还絮叨个不停的盐贩老汉，这会儿也把头埋得低低的，恨不能钻进桌子底下。

    江砚握着笔的手，慢慢攥紧了。

    这一幕，他太熟了。
content_en:
It's been half a month since my body was completely exhausted.

    Jiang Yan resumed his small livelihood. Uncle Qin bought him a palm-sized space near the wall in Xifang City, an old wooden table with missing corners, a bald inkstone, and a few pieces of rough paper, which were all his belongings. The traders and lackeys who came and went, who wanted to send messages to their homes far away, who couldn't figure out the accounting of transactions, or who couldn't understand the notices posted by the government, all came to him to ask questions. A letter costs two cents, and an account costs one cent. When money is tight, a bowl of hot soup and half a piece of cake are enough.

    Life was tight, but I finally earned it.

    At noon that day, Jiang Yan was writing a letter home for an old man who sold salt. The old man was illiterate and kept mumbling about the things he wanted to send to his wife in the countryside. They were nothing more than "Business is good this year", "Don't worry about it" and "Put on more clothes when the weather is cold". While Jiang Yan listened, he picked out the most important things to write, and sorted out those confusing household words into a few lines of smooth words.

    The pen moves steadily. He hadn't touched his golden finger for half a month, and now he was writing and tracing things honestly every day, and he felt a sense of security that he had never felt before. Uncle Qin's words were like a thorn in his heart, but they made him feel at ease.

    At the west end of Fangshi, there was a sudden commotion.

    First, someone yelled something at the top of their lungs, then there was the clatter of a stall overturning, the jingle of coins rolling to the ground, and then, a woman's cry for help.

    Jiang Yan's writing hand stopped.

    The face of the old salt seller who wrote the letter changed. He shrank his neck in a hurry, leaned towards Jiang Yan, and lowered his voice: "The man with gold teeth...is here to collect money again. Sir, don't look at it, lower your head and write yours."

    "Gold teeth?"

    "The local snake in the market." The old man's voice was trembling, but his eyes couldn't help but glance over. "He has a gold tooth in his mouth, and everyone who sees him has to call him 'Golden Tooth Master'. This Xishikou is the government's market on the surface, but secretly it belongs to him. Those who set up stalls, purchase goods, and even beg for food have to be 'filial' to him. If you give him too late or too little, the stall will be smashed in the least, and your legs will be broken in the worst."

    Jiang Yan followed the sound and looked over.

    About twenty paces away, three or four broad-shouldered men were surrounding a middle-aged woman selling needles and thread. One of them, short and fat, with his arms open, revealing his body, opened his mouth to speak, and the gold teeth in his mouth dangled in the sun, making people dizzy. He stepped on the overturned stall under his feet, with needlework, buttons, and bits of cloth scattered on the floor. The woman knelt on the ground, hurriedly moving back, crying and begging.

    "Master Jinya, this month... I really can't make up the money this month. My family is sick and the child is still young..."

    "Sick?" Jin Ya spat, "You still come out to set up a stall when you are sick? Setting up a stall means you have income. Why should you not respect me if you have income?" He kicked the small pile of goods that he had just collected away, "The rules are the rules. Today is thirty cents, not a penny less. Can't make it up? If you can't make it up, I will help you get it together -"

    He waved his hand, and the man next to him went up to lift the small cloth bag that the woman was protecting.

    "Don't move! Don't move that! That's the money for my baby's medicine—"

    The woman rushed to protect him, but was pushed away and fell to the ground.

    No one in Manfang City dared to step forward. The stall owner lowered his head to pack his goods, and the pace of passing by quickened and went around elsewhere. Even the old salt seller who was chattering non-stop just now had his head lowered, wishing he could get under the table.

    Jiang Yan's hand holding the pen slowly tightened.

    He was too familiar with this scene.
